fetched_contents.text: Weakness and Fatigue Is this your child's symptom? * Weakness means decreased muscle strength. * Paralysis means severe loss of strength. The child can't move a part of the body. * Fatigue means feeling very tired and needing extra rest. Muscle strength is normal. Symptoms of Weakness (loss of strength) * True weakness always interferes with function. Once a child is walking, weakness is seen more in the legs than the arms. Reason: muscle strength is needed for normal walking. * Leg Weakness. This is what you will see. Examples: trouble standing, walking, climbing stairs, getting off the floor, running and jumping. If severe, the child can't stand or walk. * Arm Weakness. This is what you will see. Examples: trouble feeding one's self, writing/drawing/typing, combing or washing the hair. Other children have trouble lifting objects above the head, turning door knobs or buttoning shirts. If the weakness is severe, the child starts dropping objects. * Face Weakness. Weak face muscles cause droopy eyelids or trouble moving the eyes. A droopy face or crooked smile may also occur. You might notice trouble sucking, swallowing or speaking. * Weakness in Babies. In infants not yet walking, you will see the loss of motor milestones (loss of normal development). These include new trouble turning over, sitting, crawling, and pulling up. In the early months, you will see the loss of head support, reaching or kicking. A weak cry or suck also may be seen. Causes of New Onset Muscle Weakness * Most causes of new onset muscle weakness are serious. True weakness points to diseases of the spinal cord or its nerves. Nerves carry messages from the spinal cord to the muscles in the arms and legs. Diseases that cause muscle weakness are very rare. * Most children with new onset weakness need special tests to make the right diagnosis. If the weakness gets worse, most children need to be admitted to the hospital. Specific Causes of New Onset Muscle Weakness * Polio is a severe spinal cord disease that causes paralysis. It is prevented by the polio virus vaccine. Polio is almost wiped out in the entire world. There have been no cases in the US since 1979. Now, it only occurs in 2 countries. * Acute Flaccid Myelitis (AFM) is a rare infection of the spinal cord. It acts like polio did. It causes sudden onset of arm or leg weakness in one or more places. The main cause has been an enterovirus. There has been a rise in cases since 2014. * West Nile Virus myelitis. See the Mosquito Bite care guide for details. Also acts like polio did. * Guillain-Barre syndrome is a severe nerve weakness that starts in the feet and moves up the body over several days. It affects the same parts on both sides of the body. It can follow some viral infections. * Tick paralysis is a rare problem from a tick that has been attached for 5 or more days. Often it is hidden in the hair. Once the tick is removed, the weakness clears. It takes a few hours to a day. * Poisoning. Some types of poisoning can cause weakness, often with confusion. * Viral myositis. Muscle pain in the leg muscles is seen with some viral infections, such as influenza. The pain can make some children not want to walk. This is different than weakness. fetched_contents.title: Approach to the child with fatigue: A focus for the general pediatrician - PMC
fetched_contents.text: Approach to the child with fatigue: A focus for the general pediatrician Abstract Background Fatigue is a common, nonspecific complaint commonly used to describe various conditions, ranging from a vague, subjective sense of weariness to muscular weakness, fatigability, exercise intolerance or excessive daytime somnolence. Despite its high frequency in the general population, literature addressing the approach to the child with fatigue from a general pediatrician perspective is poor. We herein propose a review of the available evidence on the topic, providing a practical framework to assist physicians in dealing with the issue. Methods Data were identified by searches of MEDLINE, UpToDate, Google Scholar and references from relevant articles. Articles published between 1990 and 2021 were considered, prioritizing systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Then, an empirically-based model of approaching the tired child was proposed according to our center experience. Results To correctly characterize the meaning of fatigue reporting, specific clues from history and physical examination should be emphasized. Duration, severity, and the age at onset are to be considered. Then, specific queries about everyday activities, sleep hygiene and social domain could be useful in reaching a specific diagnosis and offering an appropriate treatment. Conclusions We suggest a pragmatic approach to fatigue in children based on age assessment, targeted questions, physical examination clues, and some laboratory first-level tests. This could provide pediatricians with a useful tool to discriminate the broad etiology of such a complaint, disentangling between psychological and organic causes. Further studies are needed to investigate the predictive value, specificity and sensitivity of this diagnostic workflow in managing the child with fatigue. Keywords: fatigue, tiredness, fatigability, weakness, tired child, weariness, drowsiness Introduction Tiredness, weariness, weakness, fatigability and fatigue are words commonly used in the everyday vocabulary, sometimes mistakenly as synonyms, to describe a sense of difficulty or inability to initiate, maintain or complete tasks which require mental and/or physical energy. However, such different meanings should not be interchangeable to the physician. For example, the reduced capacity to maintain an activity, defined as easy fatigability and evocative of a myasthenic syndrome, should be distinguished from the inability to initiate or perform a specific action, which may underlie a neurological or muscular disease. Also, discriminating between psychological and physical tiredness can be challenging, especially among adolescent patients. Furthermore, fatigue can be secondary to an almost unlimited range of acute and chronic diseases encompassing cardiological, pulmonary, endocrinological, gastrointestinal, nephrological, rheumatological and metabolic conditions, cancer, and psychological/psychiatric comorbidities (1–7). Due to the broad etiology and subjectivity of its reports, the epidemiology of fatigue is also rather challenging to define. A generic complaint of fatigue represents about 10%–15% of primary care consultations among adults (8). Notably, in adults, chronic fatigue is strongly associated with psychiatric disorders, with two-thirds of people suffering from long-lasting fatigue being also affected by psychiatric comorbidities (9). The prevalence of children complaining of fatigue falls to about 4.4%, depending on sex and age, with the highest frequency amongst adolescent females (10, 11). Remarkably, the reported number of pediatric patients complaining of psychological fragility has continuously been increasing in the last decades (12–14). Recent studies found fatigue to be more prevalent in children affected by chronic diseases, reaching a rate of 21.2% in those with cystic fibrosis, autoimmune diseases and post-cancer treatment, and 25% in pediatric rheumatic disease (15, 16). The available literature has mainly focused on quantifying and managing fatigue in the broader context of childhood chronic diseases (3–6, 17), while less is written on the definition and categorization of fatigue complaint per se. Another significant proportion of studies deals with chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), a blurred defined and debated clinical entity, with specific diagnostic criteria and significant overlap with psychiatric and functional disorders (18, 19). Due to the inherent subjectivity of the symptom, quantification and assessment of fatigue is even more challenging in the pediatric population for the possible ambivalence between patient's and parental reports (20). Physicians, in their daily practice, use age criteria, history and physical examination clues to discriminate the different hypotheses and establish if and which tests are to be performed. However, despite the high frequency of such a complaint, we are not aware of any study or review suggesting a general pediatric guideline in this perspective. Applying a diagnostic algorithm to the symptom of fatigue could help to discriminate its multiple causes, possibly leading, on the one hand, to an early diagnosis of specific organic conditions and, on the other, to the timely unmasking of possible mental health problems. The latter is especially relevant, as symptom persistence is reported to lead to prolonged school absence, isolation and loss of activities resulting in the risk of academic failure and development of psychiatric conditions in adult age (21–23). This work aims to review the available evidence on the topic and provide a pragmatic framework to assist the pediatrician in dealing with the child complaining of fatigue as the main isolated symptom, both in primary care setting and in the emergency department. Further studies will be needed to assess the effectiveness of this approach and improve it. Likely diagnoses and what they could mean

The evidence points to a broad spectrum of possibilities, but the most important distinction is that muscle weakness and fatigue in a 7-year-old are not benign unless the child is simply “very tired” from normal illness. The Seattle Children’s Hospital source says that “diseases that cause muscle weakness are very rare” and that “most children with new onset weakness need special tests to make the right diagnosis” [N1-F1]. That is a strong signal: the patient’s symptoms should not be dismissed as a simple explanation, but they should also not be assumed to be an immediately life-threatening emergency unless the history clearly warrants it.

### Most common and serious possible causes

The most serious possibilities in the evidence are the rare but important neurological and metabolic conditions, especially when the weakness is recent, progressive, or associated with other red flags. The same source lists AFM, tick paralysis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, West Nile virus myelitis, poisoning, and polio as examples of causes that act like polio and require urgent evaluation [N1-F1]. It also says that “true weakness always interferes with function” and that “most children with new onset weakness need special tests” [N1-F1]. That is especially relevant because the patient is already struggling to climb stairs and run normally, and is “acting tired all the time” [N1-F1].

At the same time, the evidence also emphasizes that muscle weakness can be caused by several reasons and may be a sign of a serious health condition that needs medical care [N3-R3]. So the likely diagnoses are not just one single “rare disease” but a spectrum from more common functional or developmental explanations to less common but serious organic diseases.

### Which conditions are likely versus which are less likely

The evidence supports a hierarchy of likelihood:

1. **Developmental or musculoskeletal delay** is likely if the child’s weakness is part of a broader developmental pattern. The “12+ months” child-muscle-weakness toolkit notes that weakness can result in difficulty with stair climbing, avoidance of stairs, and abnormal gait patterns such as lateral lean during stance or pronation of feet and ankles [N3-F3]. It also states that muscle weakness results in difficulty with stair climbing and that children who are weak often avoid stairs, crawl, or stop to rest when climbing [N3-F3]. This is a red flag that the child’s weakness may not be a rare disease but could be a more common delay or weakness-related motor problem.

2. **Neuromuscular disease** is less likely overall, but still important. The Seattle Children’s material says that “most causes of new onset muscle weakness are serious” and that “true weakness points to diseases of the spinal cord or its nerves” [N1-F1]. The same source also lists several rare conditions, including AFM, tick paralysis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and West Nile virus myelitis, as examples of serious causes [N1-F1]. These are less likely than developmental/musculoskeletal explanations, but they are serious enough that they should not be ignored.

3. **Metabolic or systemic disease** is also a possible explanation, though the evidence here is less direct. The broader fatigue article notes that fatigue can be secondary to a broad range of acute and chronic diseases, including endocrinological, rheumatological, and metabolic conditions, as well as cancer and psychiatric comorbidities [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not explicitly list a specific metabolic disease for the 7-year-old, it does establish that weakness and fatigue can be part of a wider systemic illness [N2-F2].

4. **Normal fatigue or overexertion** is possible but less likely given the child’s symptoms. The Seattle Children’s fatigue/fatigue-and-fatigue page says that normal fatigue can happen during illness and can make children less active, but it distinguishes normal fatigue from true weakness [N1-F1]. It also says that if the weakness gets worse, most children need to be admitted to the hospital, and that “true weakness always interferes with function” [N1-F1]. That strongly suggests that the child’s symptoms are more consistent with true muscle weakness than with ordinary tiredness after play or sport.

### What specific symptoms or signs would point to each diagnosis

The evidence provides several red flags and signs that help distinguish likely explanations:

- **Developmental/musculoskeletal delay or weakness**  
  - Difficulty climbing stairs, especially with avoidance of stairs, crawling, or stopping to rest [N3-F3]  
  - Gait abnormalities such as lateral lean during stance, pronation of feet, increased base of support, or toe walking [N3-F3]  
  - Use of arms excessively to pull up the stair railing, failure to alternate feet, or dependence on rail support [N3-F3]  
  - Delayed or regressed motor milestones in a broader developmental context [N3-F3]

- **Neurological disease or AFM-like condition**  
  - Sudden or recent onset of weakness [N1-F1]  
  - Progressive weakness or worsening weakness [N1-F1]  
  - Signs that suggest ascending paralysis, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome’s progressive weakness and areflexia [N4-R4]  
  - Any evidence of central nervous system involvement, including possible brain imaging findings [N4-R2]  

- **Tick paralysis**  
  - Weakness that improves after removal of a tick attached for 5 or more days [N1-R4]  
  - This is very specific, but the evidence is only indirect here [N1-R4]

- **Guillain-Barré syndrome**  
  - Progressive ascending weakness with areflexia [N4-R4]  
  - The evidence here is limited to the diagnostic workup reference, not a direct case description [N4-R4]

- **Metabolic or systemic disease**  
  - Fatigue that is not explained by true weakness, but the evidence here is broader and less concrete [N2-F2]  
  - The fatigue article notes that fatigue can be secondary to a wide range of acute and chronic conditions, including endocrinological and metabolic diseases [N2-F2]

- **Normal fatigue**  
  - Fatigue that does not interfere with function and is explained by a short-term illness or extra rest [N1-F1]  
  - The evidence is explicit that this is different from true weakness [N1-F1]

### Bottom line

Overall, the most likely explanation is a **developmental or musculoskeletal weakness** that is causing climbing difficulty and fatigue, especially if the child is struggling with stairs, avoiding stairs, or showing abnormal gait patterns [N3-F3]. At the same time, the evidence makes clear that **true weakness is serious** and that **most children with new onset weakness need special tests** [N1-F1]. So the most cautious interpretation is that the child should be evaluated promptly, but the family should not assume an immediately life-threatening emergency unless the history clearly supports it.

Yes — the child’s symptoms are concerning enough to warrant a medical evaluation, and the evidence supports several possible explanations. The short answer is: **this is not normal childhood tiredness, but it is not necessarily an immediately life-threatening emergency either** [N1-F1][N5-R2].

## What the symptoms could mean

The most likely explanation, based on the evidence, is a **developmental or musculoskeletal weakness** affecting climbing, running, and general strength [N3-F3]. The child’s difficulty with stairs, tiredness, and falling over are classic signs of muscle weakness, and the evidence says that weakness can be a sign of a serious health condition that needs medical care [N3-R3][N1-F1]. In other words, these are not just “boys will be boys” or minor fatigue symptoms.

At the same time, the evidence also says that **true weakness is serious** and that **most children with new onset weakness need special tests** [N1-F1]. That means the next step should be a careful evaluation rather than assuming a simple explanation.

### Which conditions are more likely versus less likely?

The evidence supports a hierarchy of likelihood:

1. **Developmental or musculoskeletal delay** is the most likely explanation in this context. The toolkit for muscle weakness says that weakness can result in difficulty with stair climbing, avoidance of stairs, and abnormal gait patterns [N3-F3]. It also notes that muscle weakness results in difficulty with stair climbing and that children who are weak often avoid stairs, crawl, or stop to rest when climbing [N3-F3]. This pattern is consistent with a problem that is not rare but still meaningful.

2. **Neurological or metabolic disease** is less likely overall, but still important. The Seattle Children’s source says that most causes of new onset muscle weakness are serious and that true weakness points to diseases of the spinal cord or its nerves [N1-F1]. It also lists rare but serious conditions such as AFM, tick paralysis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and West Nile virus myelitis as examples of serious causes that act like polio [N1-F1]. These are less likely than developmental/musculoskeletal explanations, but they are serious enough that they should not be ignored.

3. **Normal fatigue or overexertion** is possible but less likely given the child’s symptoms. The evidence says that normal fatigue can happen during illness and can make children less active, but it distinguishes normal fatigue from true weakness [N1-F1]. The upstream branch report also notes that the symptoms are more consistent with true muscle weakness than with ordinary tiredness [N7].

## What the family should do next

The evidence supports a practical two-step approach: first, decide whether the situation is urgent or can be handled in the routine pediatric setting; second, prepare for the next evaluation with specific questions and tests [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### When to seek immediate or urgent medical attention

If any of the following red flags appear, the family should seek immediate care:

- Sudden worsening of weakness  
- New unsteady walking  
- The child looks or acts very sick  
- Trouble breathing or slow breathing  
- Any sign of acute neurological involvement  

The Seattle Children’s source explicitly says to call 911 if the child is hard to wake up, awake but can’t move, has trouble breathing, or has followed a head or neck injury [N1-F1]. It also says to call the doctor or seek care now if the child has new onset of weakness, unsteady walking, looks or acts very sick, or you think the problem is urgent [N1-F1]. So these are the signs that would tip the balance toward urgent care.

### What tests or specialist consultations are typically next

The evidence suggests a staged workup. For a child with new onset weakness, most children need special tests to make the right diagnosis [N1-F1]. The upstream branch report also notes that specialist referral is needed if red flags are present, especially to pediatric neurology [N7]. In practice, the next steps may include:

- A careful physical examination to assess muscle strength, gait, and signs of weakness [N1-F1][N4-R1]
- Laboratory tests as part of the workup for weakness and fatigue [N4-R1]
- Neuroimaging if brain pathology is suspected [N4-R2]
- Specialist referral, especially if the weakness is recent, progressive, or associated with other red flags [N3-F3][N4-R4]

The routine pediatric visit is still a reasonable first step if the symptoms are not clearly life-threatening [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### How to prepare for the appointment and what questions to ask

The evidence supports gathering a detailed history and being ready to ask specific questions. The fatigue article emphasizes that the physician should use history, physical examination, and some first-level tests to discriminate between organic and psychological causes [N2-F2]. The Seattle Children’s page also suggests noting whether the child is alert when awake, whether extra sleeping is normal, and whether the fatigue is part of a short-term illness [N1-F1].

A helpful checklist for the family includes:

- Record the child’s symptoms: when they started, how often they occur, and what makes them better or worse  
- Note any red flags: sudden worsening, new unsteady walking, child acting very sick, or trouble breathing  
- List specific activities affected: climbing stairs, running, playing, and whether the child avoids certain movements  
- Ask about sleep and energy: whether the child sleeps extra hours, is alert when awake, and needs more rest  
- Prepare questions for the doctor: whether the symptoms are likely normal fatigue, a developmental delay, or something more serious; what tests are next; and whether specialist referral is needed  

## How to explain this to the family without causing unnecessary alarm

The evidence supports a balanced reassurance: the child’s symptoms are concerning enough to warrant a doctor’s attention, but they are not necessarily an immediately life-threatening emergency unless the history clearly warrants it [N1-F1][N5-R2]. The upstream branch report also notes that the most likely explanation is a developmental or musculoskeletal weakness, while still acknowledging that true weakness can be serious and may require special tests [N7].

So a helpful way to explain it is: “It sounds like something that needs a doctor’s attention, but it’s not something that has to be an emergency right away.” You can reassure the family that it is important to get checked, but also that doctors can often figure out whether this is a normal variation, a developmental issue, or something more serious [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7].

## Signs to watch for at home

The evidence provides several signs the family should watch for at home:

- Sudden worsening of weakness  
- New unsteady walking  
- The child acting very sick  
- Trouble breathing or slow breathing  
- Any head or neck injury  
- Any sign of acute neurological involvement [N1-F1]

The upstream branch report also notes that red flags for neuromuscular disease include stair climbing difficulty, abnormal gait, and regression in motor milestones [N7]. So at home, the family should watch whether the child’s climbing or walking pattern changes, whether they avoid stairs, or whether they show signs of weakness that were not present before [N3-F3][N7].

## How to balance caution with normal childhood variation

The evidence supports caution, but it also supports distinguishing true weakness from normal tiredness. The Seattle Children’s page explicitly says that normal fatigue can happen during illness and can make children less active, but it is different from true weakness [N1-F1]. The fatigue article likewise notes that fatigue can be secondary to a broad range of conditions, including illness, chronic disease, and psychiatric comorbidities, but it emphasizes that the history and physical examination should guide the workup [N2-F2].

So the family can be reassured that they are being cautious when they seek help, while also being realistic that the child’s symptoms are meaningful and warrant evaluation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7].

## Bottom line

In short: the child’s symptoms are concerning enough to need a medical evaluation, but they are not necessarily an emergency unless the history clearly supports it [N1-F1][N5-R2]. The most likely explanation is a developmental or musculoskeletal weakness affecting climbing and running, but the evidence also makes clear that true weakness can be serious and may require special tests [N3-F3][N7]. The family should talk to the pediatrician first, watch for worsening symptoms or red flags, and be ready to ask questions about tests and specialist referral [N5-R2][N6-R3][N4-R1][N4-R2].

If the child is falling over, struggling to climb stairs, and acting tired all the time, the safest next step is to get evaluated as soon as possible — not because the problem is obviously rare, but because the symptoms are meaningful enough to need careful assessment [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7].
